Accuracy may be improved through mesh refinement, polynomial order, or both. Fewer higher-order elements can sometimes reach the accuracy of a much finer linear mesh at the cost of larger local matrices.

10791.title: Hierholzer's Algorithm
10791.heading: Hierholzer's Algorithm
10791.content:
Hierholzer's algorithm finds an [[Eulerian Circuit]] in a graph that contains one. Starting at a vertex, it follows unused edges until it returns to that vertex and forms an initial closed tour.

If a vertex on the current tour still touches an unused edge, the algorithm starts another unused-edge tour there and splices the new circuit into the old one. Repeating this process incorporates every edge. With an appropriate implementation, the work is linear in the number of edges.

A Haar transform on a binary dendrogram replaces child vectors with a parent smooth and signed detail. The smooth summarizes the two children, while the detail records their difference. Repeating this at successive merges gives one global smooth and a collection of branch-level details.

Following the correct route from root to leaf and adding or subtracting its details exactly reconstructs the original observation in the book's construction. The hierarchy is therefore not only a display of groups; it is an operational multiscale encoding of the data.

10809.title: Hierarchical Clustering
10809.heading: Hierarchical Clustering
10809.content:
Hierarchical clustering constructs nested groups ranging from singleton observations to a cluster containing the complete data set. Every pair of clusters is either disjoint or one contains the other, so the structure can be represented as a [[Dendrogram]].

The hierarchy preserves possible solutions at many resolutions. A separate decision selects the level that best serves the analysis.

The source begins with one cluster per gene-expression sample and repeatedly joins the two most similar groups. A chosen linkage rule converts pairwise sample distances into distances between clusters, while the resulting tree supports exploration without assuming the tissue labels in advance.

The book adds a contrasting way to obtain hierarchy: a Baire longest-common-prefix tree reads nested bins from an encoded value in one pass, without first evaluating every pairwise distance. This can be useful for massive collections, but its groups depend on measurement precision and any projection used to create the code. Sequence-constrained agglomeration is another variant: it permits adjacent passages to merge so a tree retains chronology as well as similarity.

The hierarchical result model uses an abstract Node with parent, identifier, and level state plus virtual operations for visitor dispatch, child count, and record count. All leaf nodes occupy level zero, while internal nodes represent successively joined or split groups.

This common interface lets clients traverse a nested clustering without branching on storage layout at every step. Parent links and levels make ancestry explicit but must be updated together during tree construction.

Keeping forest, size map, active set, and distance cache synchronized is essential. A partial update can leave the next nearest-pair search referring to a cluster that no longer exists.

Hierarchical cluster permanence is the rule that once two entities or groups merge, they remain joined at all later agglomerative levels. The merged cluster becomes a building block for subsequent decisions.

This property makes the result a true nested hierarchy, but it also propagates early mistakes. Hierarchical clustering does not perform the later reallocation used by iterative partition methods.

A hierarchy can represent one observation as successive approximations. Begin with the global smooth of a dendrogram Haar transform, then add the signed details on that observation's path. Each added branch distinction gives a finer representation until the original vector is recovered.

The book relates this sequence to a partial order of information: an ancestor-level description is less specific than a descendant-level one. Its simplified face example uses the chain to propose a way to generate an object from a group average and a short sequence of refinements; the practical value depends on the chosen hierarchy and representation.

10830.heading: Hidden Markov Model
10830.content:
A hidden Markov model represents a sequence as transitions among unobserved states that probabilistically emit observable evidence. In speech recognition, the hidden states can represent stages of a speech sound while feature vectors provide the observations.

The model captures duration and order without requiring exact time alignment. It was central to traditional [[Acoustic Model|acoustic modeling]] before end-to-end neural systems became dominant.

As a recursive Bayesian model, a hidden Markov model combines a state transition distribution with an observation distribution. The same decomposition supports filtering of the current state, prediction of later states, and smoothing of past states when later evidence is available.

Hidden Markov model classification represents a sequence through unobserved states that evolve with a Markov transition structure and emit the observed symbols or measurements. A class can be associated with a separate model or incorporated into the state structure.

Prediction compares the sequence likelihood under competing class models. Dynamic programming makes inference feasible by reusing partial calculations rather than enumerating every possible hidden-state path.

A hidden layer is a [[Neural Network Layer]] that is not directly exposed as the network's external input or final output. It transforms signals received from an earlier layer and passes its activations onward.

Multiple hidden layers let a [[Deep Neural Network]] build increasingly abstract representations. In image recognition, earlier layers may respond to local edges while later layers combine those patterns into larger structures.

10839.content:
The hidden labor of AI is the human work concealed by descriptions of an intelligent system as autonomous. People collect and label training examples, correct outputs, moderate harmful content, maintain infrastructure, and perform small tasks that make automated services possible.

Invisibility affects ethical judgment because the system appears cleaner and more capable when labor conditions are removed from view. Workers may be geographically distant, poorly paid, or exposed to disturbing material while users interact with a polished interface. Evaluating AI therefore requires following the full production chain and recognizing [[Digital Labor]] as part of the system.

10842.title: Heuristic Evaluation
10842.heading: Heuristic Evaluation
10842.content:
Heuristic evaluation is an analytic method in which several usability experts independently inspect a [[User Interface]] using general or domain-specific design guidelines. Representative users are not required.

The experts' findings are combined, ranked, and used to prioritize redesign. The method can expose major problems quickly and inexpensively, especially early in development. Its effectiveness depends on the quality and relevance of the heuristics and the expertise of the evaluators.

For a novel [[3D User Interface]], heuristic evaluation can precede user-based [[Formative Evaluation]] as part of an iterative evaluation sequence.

Shared latent representations, cross-domain relations, or paired examples can connect the spaces. The mapping becomes part of the learning problem and must preserve information relevant to the target rather than only reconstructing source structure.

10857.title: Hessian Matrix
10857.heading: Hessian Matrix
10857.content:
The Hessian matrix of a twice-differentiable function collects its second partial derivatives: $H_{ij}=\partial^2f/(\partial x_i\partial x_j)$. When mixed partials agree, the Hessian is a [[Symmetric Matrix]].

At a [[Stationary Point]], a positive-definite Hessian indicates a strict [[Local Minimum]], and a negative-definite Hessian indicates a strict [[Local Maximum]]. An indefinite Hessian is associated with a [[Saddle Point]].

10860.title: Hermitian Matrix
10860.heading: Hermitian Matrix
10860.content:
A complex square matrix is Hermitian when it equals its conjugate transpose. This generalizes a real [[Symmetric Matrix]].

Hermitian matrices have real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors associated with distinct eigenvalues. Their quadratic forms and spectral properties make them central to complex linear algebra.

10863.title: Heatmap
10863.heading: Heatmap
10863.content:
A heatmap represents the entries of a data matrix with color and commonly reorders its rows and columns through clustering. It lets many features and samples be viewed at once so blocks, gradients, outliers, and possible group structure become visible.

Color scale, transformation, feature selection, and clustering distance all affect the pattern. The source cautions that red-green palettes are difficult for many color-blind readers, making accessible encoding part of analytical communication.

10866.title: Helmholtz Finite Element Eigenproblem
10866.heading: Helmholtz Finite Element Eigenproblem
10866.content:
A Helmholtz finite element eigenproblem arises when a source-free wave equation contains an unknown wave-number parameter. Element gradient and interpolation matrices assemble into a generalized eigenvalue equation.

In a waveguide, eigenvalues approximate cutoff parameters and eigenvectors approximate field patterns of supported modes. Symmetric assembled matrices yield real eigenvalues under the stated homogeneous formulation.

10869.sourceSearchName: heisenberg uncertainty principle heisenberg uncertainty principle
10869.title: Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle
10869.heading: Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle
10869.content:
The Heisenberg uncertainty principle places a lower bound on simultaneous position and momentum spreads:

$$\Delta x\,\Delta p\geq\frac{\hbar}{2}.$$

This is not merely instrument disturbance; it reflects the structure of quantum states. A narrowly localized wave packet requires a broad range of component wavelengths and therefore momenta.

10872.heading: Heliostat

A field of individually steered heliostats concentrates sunlight at the tower of a [[Solar Tower Power Plant]]. Mirror reflectivity, aiming accuracy, shading, and intercepted fraction affect how much radiation reaches the receiver; the field's large collection area alone does not determine useful heat.

10881.heading: Heat Transfer in Solids and Fluids Interface
10881.content:
A heat-transfer interface spanning solids and fluids uses conduction in every participating domain and adds fluid energy transport where motion exists. Domain-specific material properties and sources enter one shared temperature formulation.

Used alone, the interface can approximate a fluid as a conducting domain or accept prescribed velocity information. Coupling it to a flow interface creates [[Conjugate Heat Transfer Coupling|conjugate heat transfer]] in which velocity and temperature are solved consistently.

10884.title: Heat Transfer Problem Classification
10884.heading: Heat Transfer Problem Classification
10884.content:
Thermal processes can be classified by what remains constant or what crosses the boundary. Isothermal processes hold temperature constant, isobaric processes hold pressure constant, isochoric processes hold volume constant, and adiabatic processes exclude energy transfer across the selected boundary.

Isentropic and isenthalpic descriptions instead hold entropy or enthalpy constant. These labels are modeling constraints, not interchangeable synonyms, and they help determine the governing equations, properties, and conditions required by a [[Thermal System and Control Volume|thermal system or control volume]].

10887.title: Heat Engine
10887.heading: Heat Engine
10887.content: A heat engine operates cyclically between a hot reservoir and a cold reservoir. It absorbs heat $Q_H$, converts part to useful work $W$, and rejects the remainder $Q_C$, so $W=Q_H-Q_C$. Its efficiency $W/Q_H$ is always below one and is bounded by the reservoir temperatures through the [[Second Law of Thermodynamics]].

10890.title: Heat Conduction
10890.heading: Heat Conduction
10890.content:
Heat conduction is energy transfer through a material without net motion of its mass. The heat-flow rate is governed by thermal conductivity, cross-sectional area, and the spatial temperature gradient.

Finite element conduction matrices convert this continuum relationship into nodal temperature and heat-flow equations. Material interfaces are handled by assembling elements with their own conductivities and dimensions.

10893.title: Heat as Energy in Transit
10893.heading: Heat as Energy in Transit
10893.content:
Heat is energy crossing a boundary because a temperature difference exists. It is not a substance stored inside an object; the stored quantity is internal energy, while heat describes the transfer that changes that energy.

The spontaneous direction is from higher temperature to lower temperature until [[Thermal Equilibrium and Temperature Difference|thermal equilibrium]] is approached. A heat-transfer model therefore needs both a temperature field and a boundary through which energy may enter or leave.

10908.title: Head-Worn Display
10908.heading: Head-Worn Display
10908.content:
A head-worn display is a [[Visual Display]] worn on the user's head so the imagery remains aligned with the eyes as the head moves. Opaque versions can immerse a user in [[Virtual Reality]], while see-through forms can overlay information for [[Augmented Reality]].

Head tracking lets the system render from the user's changing viewpoint. Because the display turns with the head, it can provide a 360-degree [[Field of Regard]] even when its instantaneous [[Field of View]] is much smaller.

Design tradeoffs include resolution, weight, comfort, optics, depth-cue conflicts, and [[Latency]].

For AR, a head-worn display may use an [[Optical See-Through Display|optical see-through]] combiner or a [[Video See-Through Display|video see-through]] camera pipeline. Monocular, bi-ocular, and binocular arrangements provide different [[Ocularity|ocularity]], while eye-to-display calibration and focus determine how well imagery aligns with and can be comfortably viewed beside physical objects.

10911.content:
A head-up display places indicators over the main view rather than in a separate screen area. It can show health, ammunition, objectives, maps, or other changing state while play continues.

HUD elements should be readable against varied backgrounds and should not obscure the action they are meant to support. Information belongs there only when the player needs it frequently enough to justify persistent screen space.

Common programmable HUD elements include an [[Aiming Reticle]], [[Game Radar Display]], and [[Waypoint Indicator]]. Each converts game state or world-space information into stable screen-space feedback while the main scene continues to update.

The Harris corner detector identifies locations where image intensity changes strongly in two directions. Shifting a window around a true corner produces large differences for movements along either axis, unlike an edge, which changes mainly across one direction, or a flat patch, which changes little.

These stable points provide candidate locations for clone matching. The detector reduces the search space but does not determine whether a forgery occurred; descriptors, geometric grouping, and pixel-level verification must follow.

10920.title: Hazard Ratio
10920.heading: Hazard Ratio
10920.content:
A hazard ratio is the exponentiated coefficient from a Cox proportional hazards model. It compares the instantaneous event hazard for a predictor level with that of the reference, conditional on the other model terms.

A value of one represents no hazard association, while values above or below one indicate higher or lower hazard. Its confidence interval must be interpreted under proportional hazards and should not be described as a simple probability or risk ratio.

Harmony preference is the desire for cooperative, agreeable, and socially supportive play. It is associated with agreeableness in the source's model and contrasts with attraction to direct interpersonal conflict.

A harmony-oriented design can reward assistance and shared success without eliminating meaningful tension. Competitive games should not assume that every socially motivated player wants adversarial interaction.

Memory isolation confines each executing process to an authorized region of memory. Hardware bounds or protection mechanisms block a process from reading or writing another process’s data unless access is explicitly granted.

This enforcement supports multi-user computing and sandboxes untrusted software. Removing protection checks for speed weakens assumptions made by operating systems and shifts security burdens to less reliable software monitoring.

A hardening Sprint closes the gap between the quality required of each ordinary increment and the broader conditions required for a release. It can address final certification, deployment preparation, accumulated polish, and defects that were not unfinished story work.

It should not become a recurring container for integration or basic quality that every Sprint was expected to provide. A large hardening burden signals a weak [[Definition of Done]].

10941.content:
Hardcoded add-on data stores vertices, faces, and related values directly in Python collections, then passes them into a new Blender mesh. This can tightly integrate a geometric template with the transformations and subsets an algorithm applies to it.

The same coupling is the method's weakness. Large numeric arrays clutter source code, are difficult for artists to replace, and can usually be read from an external interchange file instead. Hardcoding is most defensible when the data is small or inseparable from the algorithm, not merely because it avoids shipping another file.

10944.title: Haptic Display
10944.heading: Haptic Display
10944.content:
A haptic display is an [[Output Device]] that simulates physical interaction with virtual objects through touch and proprioception. Depending on its design, it can produce force, vibration, pressure, temperature, or combinations of these sensations.

Tactile feedback stimulates receptors in the skin, while kinesthetic feedback acts through muscles and joints. Effective haptic interaction requires a fast loop between user motion and returned force or touch; excessive [[Latency]] can make feedback unstable or unrealistic.

Important characteristics include [[Spatial Resolution]], temporal resolution, range, safety, attachment effort, weight, and freedom of movement. No single haptic device is best for every task.

AR haptics can exploit contact with real objects as passive feedback or add active tactile and force effects. Because the physical environment already resists motion, a design must align generated feedback with visible and tangible surfaces rather than treating touch as an independent channel.

The Handspring Treo combined personal-digital-assistant functions with cellular calling and messaging. Its 2002 design integrated the two roles more coherently than many earlier hybrid devices.

The Treo helped establish the smartphone as a distinct product category. Its success depended on interface design as well as advances in processors and radio networks.

10950.title: Handoff
10950.heading: Handoff

A handoff transfers work and responsibility from one person or discipline to another. Each handoff can introduce a queue, information loss, delayed feedback, and ambiguity about who owns the outcome.

Cross-discipline teams and smaller batches reduce these costs by increasing direct collaboration and keeping work centered on integrated features. Remaining handoffs should be visualized and measured as part of the flow.

10959.title: Halting Problem
10959.heading: Halting Problem
10959.content:
The halting problem asks whether a given [[Turing Machine]] will eventually halt on a specified input. No Turing machine or general computer program can answer this question correctly for every machine-input pair.

The proof encodes machines, assumes a decider, and constructs a machine whose behavior contradicts that decider when applied to its own indexed input. The associated halting language is [[Recursively Enumerable Language|recursively enumerable]] but not [[Recursive Language|recursive]], while its complement is not recursively enumerable.

10965.heading: Half-Life
10965.content: Half-life is the time required for the number of undecayed radioactive nuclei, or their activity, to fall to half its initial value. For decay constant $\lambda$, $t_{1/2}=\ln2/\lambda$. Each successive half-life removes half of what remains, producing exponential rather than linear decline.

10968.title: Half-Angle Identities
10968.heading: Half-Angle Identities
10968.content:
Rearranging the cosine [[Double-Angle Identities]] yields

$$\sin^2\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{1-\cos\theta}{2},\qquad
\cos^2\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{1+\cos\theta}{2}.$$

Taking square roots requires a sign chosen from the quadrant of the half-angle. The identities reduce functions of half an angle to functions of the original angle.

10971.title: Hadoop YARN
10971.heading: Hadoop YARN
10971.content:
Hadoop YARN separates cluster-wide resource management from the application-specific logic that schedules and monitors an individual job. A central resource manager allocates containers, while an application master coordinates one application's execution.

This separation lets the cluster support processing models beyond classic MapReduce and allows different frameworks to share the same managed resources.

10974.title: Gyroscope Input
10974.heading: Gyroscope Input
10974.content:
Gyroscope input measures the device's rotation rate around its axes. Integrated over time, it helps estimate changes in orientation, though accumulated error makes sensor fusion useful.

Device-motion APIs combine gyroscope and [[Accelerometer Input]] to expose attitude as Euler angles, a matrix, or a quaternion. This lets gameplay use orientation without reconstructing it from raw sensor readings alone.

10977.title: Hadoop Ecosystem
10977.heading: Hadoop Ecosystem
10977.content:
The Hadoop ecosystem is the collection of storage, resource-management, query, scripting, ingestion, coordination, and analytical tools built around distributed Hadoop clusters. Its components specialize rather than forcing one engine to solve every data task.

That flexibility creates integration and tuning work: formats, metadata, schedulers, serialization, security, and engine versions must agree across the pipeline.

10980.title: Gut-on-a-Chip
10980.heading: Gut-on-a-Chip
10980.content:
A gut-on-a-chip cultures intestinal epithelial cells under flow and cyclic deformation that mimic aspects of peristalsis. The cells can form villus-like folds and a selective barrier.

Introducing selected microbes allows the platform to study how microbiota, movement, and the epithelium interact without attempting to recreate the entire digestive system.

10983.title: Guaranteed Message Delivery
10983.heading: Guaranteed Message Delivery
10983.content:
Guaranteed message delivery is a service promise that a message will be delivered under stated conditions even if the sender or receiver becomes temporarily unavailable. Persistence retains the message while it is in transit or awaiting reception.

The book describes this level as once-and-once-only delivery. An implementation must make the scope of that promise explicit, including how it identifies a message and what happens if a receiver fails after beginning work.

10986.title: Gröbner Basis
10986.heading: Gröbner Basis
10986.content:
A Gröbner basis is a finite subset of a polynomial ideal whose leading terms generate the ideal's [[Initial Ideal]] for a chosen [[Monomial Order]]. It generates the original ideal as well.

Reduction by a Gröbner basis gives a decisive ideal-membership test: a polynomial lies in the ideal when its remainder is zero. [[Buchberger's Algorithm]] constructs a basis by resolving incompatible leading-term reductions.

10989.title: Grouping Variable
10989.heading: Grouping Variable
10989.content:
A grouping variable combines source values into a smaller set of analytically meaningful categories. Its design may distinguish exposure levels, collapse sparse or unknown categories, or align the data with a comparison planned for tables and models.

The mapping should be written as a table before it is coded and checked afterward with a contingency table against the source variable. Grouping improves interpretability but can discard information, so category boundaries need a substantive rationale.

10992.title: Growth Factor Cost
10992.heading: Growth Factor Cost
10992.content:
Growth factor cost is the expense of purified signaling proteins added to culture media to maintain proliferation or guide differentiation. These proteins can account for most of a defined medium's cost.

Large-scale food production may use lower-purity, more efficient, or alternative formulations than therapeutic manufacturing, provided they remain safe and consistently produce the required cells.

10995.title: Grouping Symbols
10995.heading: Grouping Symbols
10995.content:
Grouping symbols such as parentheses (( )), brackets ([ ]), and braces ({ }) specify which part of an expression is treated as a unit. Operations inside the innermost group are evaluated before operations acting on the group.

Grouping can override ordinary precedence and preserve the intended base of a power. For example, ((3+2)^2=25), while (3+2^2=7). Removing symbols is safe only when the surrounding operation permits it. A preceding negative sign changes every term inside the group through [[Suppression of Parentheses]].

10998.title: Grouped Distribution Plot
10998.heading: Grouped Distribution Plot
10998.content:
A grouped distribution plot compares a continuous measurement across categories, often with side-by-side box plots. The outcome appears on the measurement axis and the grouping variable determines the separate visual summaries.

The graph supports decisions about group differences, spread, and possible violations of equal-variance assumptions. Category labels should use substantive names rather than raw codes so the comparison can be interpreted without consulting the data dictionary.

11001.title: Group
11001.heading: Group
11001.content:
A group is a set with an associative binary operation, an identity element, and an inverse for every element. The operation need not be commutative.

Groups model symmetry and reversible composition, including permutations, modular addition, and nonzero field elements under multiplication.

11004.title: Group-Structured Feature Selection
11004.heading: Group-Structured Feature Selection
11004.content:
Group-structured feature selection treats predefined sets of variables as related units. Selection can retain or discard a group together when domain knowledge says its members describe one source, pathway, sensor, or representation.

This structure changes the optimization target from isolated feature relevance to coordinated inclusion. It can produce more coherent models and exploit known relationships, although a poorly defined group may force useful and noisy variables to move together.

11007.title: Group Order
11007.heading: Group Order
11007.content:
The order of a finite group is its number of elements, written |G|. Lagrange's theorem makes subgroup and element orders divide the group order.

Group order constrains possible structures but does not by itself determine a group up to isomorphism.
